chunks: I said to him (peace be upon him): 'Ibn Abi Layla asks me to testify that this is the house in which a certain person died and left as his inheritance, and that there is no heir for him other than the one for whom we have testified.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'Testify with what is in your knowledge.'
I said: 'Ibn Abi Layla makes us swear the al-ghamus oath.' He said: 'Swear — it is only based on your knowledge.'

key_terms.الشَّهَادَة: Testimony in a legal/judicial context — one of the most important instruments of Islamic procedural law
key_terms.الْغَمُوس: Al-ghamus: literally 'the immersing' oath — a solemn oath used in court that typically implies something beyond one's certain knowledge; here rendered permissible because it is confined to one's actual knowledge
key_terms.عِلْمُك: Your knowledge — the epistemological standard for both testimony and oath; the Imam emphasizes personal knowledge as the sole criterion

ai.seo_question: What does the Imam say about testifying and swearing oaths in inheritance disputes?
ai.summary: Mu'awiya ibn Wahb reports asking Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) about being compelled by the judge Ibn Abi Layla to give testimony and swear an oath in an inheritance case. The Imam's guidance is consistent and principled: both testimony and oath-taking must be confined strictly to what the witness actually knows — nothing more. This hadith addresses a legal tension where a judicial authority (Ibn Abi Layla was a famous Sunni judge of Kufa) pressured witnesses to go beyond their knowledge, and the Imam clarifies that even the al-ghamus oath — typically a false oath — becomes permissible when it reflects one's genuine knowledge.
